1.note: See how you translated the expression “burden” in [13:1](ta:13). Alternate translation: [A message about]

Isaiah is using the phrase **Behold Damascus** to express a strong feeling of urgency and warning as he introduces God’s judgment against the city. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Look! Damascus]

3.note: The expression **will be ceased** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And the fortification will cease from Ephraim]

Isaiah is not referring to a specific **fortification**. He means fortifications or fortified cities in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And fortifications will cease from Ephraim]

Isaiah is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and the kingdom will be ceased from Damascus] or [and the kingdom will cease from Damascus]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the glory of the sons of Israel** will be diminished, so the **remnant of Aram** will also lose what made them great. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And the remnant of Aram will lose their greatness just as the sons of Israel will lose their glory]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [like how glorious are]

Isaiah is speaking as if the people of **Israel** were actually the **sons** of the patriarch Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Israel] or [the people of Israel]

4.note: Isaiah is using the phrase translated as **And it will happen** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
To translate the phrase in that day here and in the rest of this chapter, see how you translated it in [4:1](ta:04).

4.q: יִדַּ֖ל כְּב֣וֹד יַעֲקֹ֑ב וּ⁠מִשְׁמַ֥ן בְּשָׂר֖⁠וֹ יֵרָזֶֽה
4.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [the glory of Jacob will become thin; indeed, the fatness of his flesh will become lean]

Isaiah is speaking as if the **glory of Jacob** were a living thing that could lose volume and become **thin**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the splendor of Jacob will diminish]

Isaiah is speaking as if the prosperity of Israel were **fatness** of a living body that could lose volume and become **lean**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his ability to prosper will diminish]

5.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a harvester** strips a field bare when **gathering standing grain**, so the judgment will strip Israel of its people and wealth. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [And Israel will be stripped clean, as when a harvester gathers the standing grain]

5.q: וְ⁠הָיָ֗ה כֶּֽ⁠אֱסֹף֙ קָצִ֣יר קָמָ֔ה וּ⁠זְרֹע֖⁠וֹ שִׁבֳּלִ֣ים יִקְצ֑וֹר וְ⁠הָיָ֛ה כִּ⁠מְלַקֵּ֥ט שִׁבֳּלִ֖ים בְּ⁠עֵ֥מֶק רְפָאִֽים
5.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of clauses in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [And it will be like a harvester gathering standing grain, and his arm reaps heads of grain; indeed, it will be like the gleaning of heads of grain in the Valley of the Raphaites]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the gleaning of heads of grain in the Valley of the Raphaites** leaves a field completely bare, so the judgment will leave very few people remaining in Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly.

6.note: The expression **will be left** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And they will leave gleanings in it]

6.q: כְּ⁠נֹ֣קֶף זַ֔יִת שְׁנַ֧יִם שְׁלֹשָׁ֛ה גַּרְגְּרִ֖ים בְּ⁠רֹ֣אשׁ אָמִ֑יר אַרְבָּעָ֣ה חֲמִשָּׁ֗ה בִּ⁠סְעִפֶ֨י⁠הָ֙ פֹּֽרִיָּ֔ה
6.note: The point of this comparison is that just as only a few olives remain after **the shaking of an olive tree**, so only a few people will remain in Israel after the judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like the few olives left after shaking an olive tree to harvest the olives]

7.note: If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [When that day comes]

Here the masculine term **a man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [a person will gaze at their Maker]

Isaiah is using **his eyes** to represent the whole person in the act of looking to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they will look to the Holy One of Israel]

Isaiah is not using this possessive form **of Israel** to indicate that the people of Israel possess or control Yahweh. Rather Isaiah is using these words to indicate that Yahweh is the God whom the Israelites worship. Alternate translation: [the holy God whom the people of Israel worship]

8.note: Isaiah is using one part of this representative man, his **hands**, to mean the man himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [his own work]

Isaiah is using another part of this representative man, his **fingers**, also to mean the man himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [what he has made]

9.note: Isaiah is using the possessive form to describe **cities** that are characterized by **strength**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [his strong cities] or [his fortified cities]

Isaiah is using the passive verbal form **abandoned**, which functions here as an adjective, as a noun to mean a certain kind of city. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [like cities that people have abandoned to the forest and the bough]

The phrase **the forest and the bough** expresses a single idea. The word **bough** tells more about **forest**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [the boughs of the forest]

Isaiah is using **from the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “because of” or “on account of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [because of the sons of Israel] or [because the sons of Israel conquered them]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **desolation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a desolate place]

10.q: שָׁכַ֨חַתְּ֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׁעֵ֔⁠ךְ וְ⁠צ֥וּר מָעֻזֵּ֖⁠ךְ לֹ֣א זָכָ֑רְתְּ
10.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **salvation** and **refuge**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [you have forgotten the God who saves you, and you have not remembered the rock that shelters you]

Isaiah is speaking as if God were a **rock** that provides safety and shelter. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and you have not remembered the one who gives you refuge]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pleasantness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [pleasant plants]

11.note: The expression **being afflicted** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [when enemies are afflicting you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **pain**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and you suffer without relief]

12.note: Isaiah is using the phrase **Woe to the multitude of many peoples** to express a strong feeling of warning and judgment against the nations. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How terrible it will be for the multitude of many peoples]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the seas** are loud and powerful when they rage, so **the many peoples** are loud and overwhelming when they rage in attack. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly.

The point of this comparison is that just as **mighty waters** produce a deafening roar, so **the multitude of many peoples** produces an overwhelming noise as it advances. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly.

13.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **many waters** produce a powerful roar, so **the peoples** are loud and threatening. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [Like the roar of many waters, so the peoples roar]

13.q: לְאֻמִּ֗ים כִּ⁠שְׁא֞וֹן מַ֤יִם רַבִּים֙ יִשָּׁא֔וּ⁠ן וְ⁠גָ֥עַר בּ֖⁠וֹ
13.note: Isaiah uses the word **but** here to indicate a contrast between the threatening power of the nations and God’s decisive defeat of them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [The peoples roar like the roar of many waters, yet he will rebuke him]

The pronoun **he** in **he will rebuke** refers to Yahweh, while **him** and the second **he** in **he will flee** refer to the enemy. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but Yahweh will rebuke the enemy, and the enemy will flee]

The expression **he will be pursued** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will pursue him]

The point of this comparison is that just as **chaff** on the mountains is easily scattered by the wind, so the enemy will be easily scattered by God’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as easily as the wind blows chaff off the mountains]

Isaiah is using **to the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “before” or “in front of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the wind]

The point of this comparison is that just as **tumbleweed** is blown away by a whirlwind, so the enemy will be driven away by God’s judgment. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and like tumbleweed that a whirlwind drives away]

Isaiah is using **to the face of** as a common expression of the culture to mean “before” or “in front of.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [before the whirlwind]

14.note: Isaiah is referring to the entire night by naming its two boundaries, **the time of evening** and **Before morning**, to emphasize the swiftness of the enemy’s destruction. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [As night approaches … before dawn]

Isaiah is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look, terror]

Isaiah is using **he is not** as a common expression of the culture to mean “he has ceased to exist” or “he is gone.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he is gone] or [he is no more]

The phrases **portion of our plunderers** and **lot of our looters** mean similar things. Isaiah is using the two phrases together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [This is what our plunderers and our looters get for their effort]
